claims.text: Atomic size mismatch produces lattice distortion in near-equiatomic multi-element solid-solution nanoparticles.
Lattice distortion acts as a kinetic barrier to atomic diffusion at elevated temperature.
Lattice distortion inhibits phase segregation at elevated temperature.
The initial nanoparticles are solid solutions with uniform elemental distributions.
Changing elemental makeup can systematically vary atomic size mismatch while retaining near-equiatomic ratios.
Greater atomic size mismatch produces greater lattice distortion.
Catalytic service is represented by exposure at 773–1173 K.
Thermoelectric service is represented by exposure at 473–1923 K.
Atomic-size-mismatch-induced strain fields lower the diffusion rates of constituent elements.
The local strain fields reduce the thermodynamic driving force for phase segregation and chemical inhomogeneity.
Reduced elemental diffusion preserves the solid solution during high-temperature exposure.
Nanoparticles with greater measured lattice distortion will retain a more uniform elemental distribution than low-distortion nanoparticles.
Nanoparticles with greater measured lattice distortion will exhibit less phase separation and chemical segregation than the baseline.
The proposed stabilization mechanism applies primarily to near-equiatomic compositions under controlled, non-extreme atmospheres.
Aggressive oxidation or reduction can cause other degradation mechanisms to dominate.
Large deviations from equiatomic composition can cause other degradation mechanisms to dominate.
Surface oxidation may modulate the relationship between lattice distortion and stability.

contradictions.description: The intervention changes elemental makeup, whereas the experiment says samples will differ only in atomic size mismatch. Changing element identities also changes chemistry, bonding, oxidation behavior, crystal preference, and diffusion properties, so size mismatch is not independently isolated.

The hypothesis frames stabilization as a kinetic diffusion barrier, but the mechanism additionally says this lowers the driving force for segregation. A kinetic barrier lowers the rate of approaching equilibrium and does not by itself lower the thermodynamic driving force.
